lesson.menu_title: The Person Who Decides — Describing People Precisely
lesson.menu_desc: One small word, two commas, and three sentences become one -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- The Person Who Decides
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 14 -- The Person Who Decides

listenings.text: The most common mistake people make before an important meeting is preparing for the wrong person. You prepare for whoever invited you, because that is who you have been emailing, and then you walk into a room where somebody else decides. Here is how you find them, and it takes about ninety seconds. The person who decides usually speaks least. They let the others ask, they listen, and everybody looks at them for half a second before answering anything. That look is the whole signal. So in the first two minutes, do not talk. Work out who the questions are really for, and from then on answer to that person, politely, without ignoring anybody else in the room.

Before Thursday, three quick things about the family, because it is not obvious from the emails. The person who signs is the sister. She has signed everything for eleven years and she will sign this. The brother is easygoing and he asks the friendliest questions in the room, and I want to be honest with you, none of them are the ones that matter. And they always bring a lawyer, who says almost nothing for forty minutes. Do not relax when she is quiet. The two questions she asks at the end are always the difficult ones, and they are always about the fees. Prepare that page.

extra_audio.text: Sonia asks Janderson whether he knows who is coming in. He says three people are coming and that he has never met any of them. Sonia tells him the woman who sits in the middle is the one who decides. She adds that the other two are her brother and a lawyer they bring to everything. She warns him that the woman comes across as cold and is not.

reading.rtitle: The Person Who Answers the Email
paras: Before any meeting that matters, somebody spends two minutes explaining who will be in the room, and those two minutes decide more than the first half hour does. There is usually one person who decides, one who signs, and one who asks the difficult questions, and they are almost never the same person.

The person who answers your emails is often none of the three. They are the one with time, which is not the same as the one with authority, and preparing an entire meeting for them is the most common and most expensive mistake in this kind of work.

Describing all that in your own language takes about fifteen seconds. Describing it in a second language often takes three separate sentences, one per person, and by the third one the other side has stopped listening. That is not a vocabulary problem. It is one small word, repeated: the one who decides, the lawyer that they bring, the report I sent yesterday.

The commas do the rest of the work. The client who signed last week is coming tells you which client, out of several. Mr Prado, who signed last week, is coming tells you something extra about a man you already know. Same words, two commas, two different sentences, and in a room where somebody is deciding about money that difference is not decoration.
reading.source: Article -- a column on meetings in a business magazine

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: You should always prepare for the person who invited you
Knowing exactly who does what in a room matters, and describing it precisely takes one small word rather than three sentences
Meetings are usually decided before they start
